summary: Describes the Network File System protocol, which Sun Microsystems and others were already using, so that others may benefit from it. It also discusses some design issues, and notes that a new version of the protocol was under development. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine opening a file that lives on another computer as if it were on your own desk. This writes down the rules that make that trick work.

questions: network file system protocol version 2 specification
what is the nfs version 2 protocol
subtitle: How Sun's Network File System lets a computer use files stored on another machine as if they were local.

tldr.problem: Users want to read and write files that live on another machine, across different operating systems and networks, without servers becoming complicated or fragile when something crashes.
tldr.mechanism: NFS version 2 defines a small set of remote procedures (lookup, read, write, create and so on) carried over Sun RPC with XDR encoding. The server keeps no protocol state, so a client can simply retry a request until the server answers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents a protocol Sun Microsystems and others were already using, and says a version three was under preparation. It is Informational, not a standard.

today: RFC 1094 is an Informational document describing version two of NFS, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. The text itself says a version three of the protocol was under preparation.

sections.title: What NFS Is
sections.content:
The Sun Network Filesystem (NFS) protocol provides transparent remote access to shared files across networks. It is designed to be portable across different machines, operating systems, network architectures and transport protocols. Implementations already existed for machines from personal computers to supercomputers.

That portability comes from building on Sun's Remote Procedure Call (RPC), described in RFC 1057, and the eXternal Data Representation (XDR) standard, described in RFC 1014. A remote procedure is identified by the host address, a program number and a procedure number. NFS is one such program, and a goal was not to require any particular level of reliability from the layers below.

The memo's status section says it describes a protocol that Sun Microsystems and others are using, that a new version is under development, and that others may benefit from the description and the discussion of design issues.
sections.plainLanguage: NFS is a way for one computer to ask another computer for its files, using a fixed set of polite requests that every machine understands.

sections.title: Stateless Servers and the File System Model
sections.content:
NFS was intended to be as stateless as possible: a server should not need to keep any protocol state about its clients in order to work correctly. After a crash or a network hiccup, a client only has to retry a request until the server responds. A client of a stateful server must instead detect the failure and rebuild the server's state, or let operations fail. The RFC accepts some extra protocol complexity in return for very simple servers that need no crash recovery.

To make retries safe, operations are made as idempotent as possible, meaning they can be repeated. Most operations, such as Read and Write, are. Some, such as remove, rename, link, mkdir and rmdir, are marked as possibly non-idempotent. Inherently stateful things such as file locking and remote execution were left to separate services.

NFS assumes a hierarchical file system in which each directory entry has a string name, and files are unstructured streams of uninterpreted bytes. Names are looked up one pathname component at a time, because operating systems use different separators and the RFC chose not to define a network standard pathname. Every operation refers to files through an opaque file handle, which can hold whatever the server needs to identify one file.

All procedures are synchronous. When a WRITE returns, the client may assume the data is on stable storage and can discard its copy, even if the server later crashes.
sections.plainLanguage: The server is like a librarian with no memory of you. Every time you ask, you hand over everything it needs, so if it forgets or you ask twice, nothing goes wrong.

sections.title: The Procedures
sections.content:
Version two of the protocol is program number 100003 and defines procedures numbered 0 to 17. NFSPROC_NULL does no work and exists to test server response and timing. GETATTR and SETATTR read and change file attributes, and LOOKUP turns a name inside a directory into a file handle plus attributes.

READ returns up to count bytes starting at offset, and WRITE writes data at an offset; a write is atomic and is not mixed with data from another client's write. CREATE, REMOVE, RENAME, LINK, SYMLINK, MKDIR and RMDIR change the directory tree, and READLINK returns the contents of a symbolic link.

READDIR returns a batch of directory entries up to a byte count. Each entry carries a cookie, an opaque pointer to the next entry, and a cookie of zero starts at the beginning of the directory. STATFS reports file system sizes such as block size and free blocks.

Some items are already marked for removal: ROOT is obsolete (the mount protocol finds the root file handle instead), WRITECACHE is for the next revision, and arguments such as totalcount are unused. Every reply starts with a stat status, where NFS_OK is 0 and the error codes derive from UNIX error numbers, for example NFSERR_NOENT (2), NFSERR_ACCES (13) and NFSERR_STALE (70, the file handle no longer refers to an existing file).
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is a menu of about eighteen things you can ask for: look up a file, read some of it, write some, make a folder, and so on. Each answer starts with a yes or a reason for no.

sections.title: Permissions and RPC Details
sections.content:
Strictly, NFS does not define how servers check permissions. The expectation is ordinary operating system checking based on AUTH_UNIX style authentication, where the server receives the client's effective uid, gid and groups on each call. This implies client and server share the same user and group numbering. The service accepts AUTH_UNIX, AUTH_DES or AUTH_SHORT, and the NULL procedure also allows AUTH_NONE.

Statelessness forces some adjustments. Because the server does not know a file is open, it checks permission on every read and write, so the server should let a file's owner access it regardless of the permission bits. For demand paging, the server allows reading if the caller has either execute or read permission. The UNIX server by default maps user id 0 to -2, so that anyone who becomes super-user on a workstation does not gain access to every remote file.

NFS is normally supported on UDP and currently uses UDP port 2049, which the RFC notes is not an officially assigned port. The memo has no separate security section.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks your ID card on every single request, because it does not remember that you already showed it a minute ago.

sections.title: Implementation Issues and Limits
sections.content:
The protocol was designed in a UNIX environment, so many operations resemble UNIX file system behavior. A stateless server cannot support removing a file that is still open, so a client can rename the file on remove and delete it only on close. Clients may not cross a server's mount point: if the server has mounted another file system on a directory, a LOOKUP shows the underlying directory instead.

Fixed limits are given as XDR constants: at most 8192 bytes of data in a READ or WRITE, pathnames up to 1024 bytes, file names up to 255 bytes, a 4-byte READDIR cookie and a 32-byte file handle. Transfers of 8192 bytes suit a local network but may cause IP fragmentation, so slower networks or gateways often do better with 512 or 1024 bytes.

Mounts may be soft, returning errors when RPC operations fail after optional retransmissions, or hard, retransmitting forever. Because a dropped reply to a remove can make a retry return NFSERR_NOENT, clients and servers may keep a small cache of recent operations; even a single entry would solve most problems.
sections.plainLanguage: There are size limits, like only carrying so many pages at once. If a request seems lost you can give up after a few tries (soft) or keep asking forever (hard).

sections.title: The Mount Protocol
sections.content:
A separate mount protocol (program number 100005, version 1) handles the operating system specific work of getting started: looking up server pathnames, validating the user and checking access permissions. Clients use it to obtain the first file handle, the only information the two protocols exchange. Keeping it apart lets new access checking methods be plugged in without changing the NFS protocol.

Its procedures are MNT (returns the file handle for a directory and records a mount entry), DUMP (lists mounts), UMNT and UMNTALL (remove entries) and EXPORT (lists exported file systems and the groups allowed to import them). The mount list is advisory, for example to warn clients that a server is going down, so it is the one place the definition implies stateful servers without affecting correctness. The mount service uses AUTH_UNIX and AUTH_NONE, runs over UDP and TCP, and its port is found through the server's portmapper described in RFC 1057.
sections.plainLanguage: The mount protocol is the front desk. You tell it which folder you want, it hands you a ticket, and you use that ticket for everything afterward.
